title: Kevin Warsh Takes the Chair at a Fed Nobody Agrees On. For NRI Investors, This Week Changes Everything.
excerpt: The new Fed chair's first meeting lands as inflation hits a three-year high, Iran peace sends oil tumbling, and the rupee claws back toward 94. The dot plot may already have shifted under him.
body:
Kevin Warsh was sworn in as chair of the Federal Reserve on May 22. Three weeks later, he walks into the most consequential debut in modern Fed history. The Federal Open Market Committee meets Tuesday and Wednesday, June 16-17, and while nobody expects a rate change — the federal funds rate will almost certainly stay at 3.50% to 3.75% — the real action will be in everything else: the updated dot plot, the Summary of Economic Projections, and Warsh's first press conference.

For the 4.5 million Indians living in the United States, and the millions more who send money home, invest across borders, or hold dollar-denominated deposits, this meeting is not academic. It will shape the dollar-rupee exchange rate, the yield on FCNR deposits, the direction of Indian equity flows, and the broader appetite for emerging-market assets for the rest of 2026.

## The Backdrop Has Changed Completely

When Warsh accepted President Trump's nomination in January, markets were pricing in rate cuts. Inflation was declining, the job market was soft, and the easing narrative was alive. The three-month war with Iran demolished all of that.

US headline inflation hit 4.2% in May, a three-year high, driven largely by energy prices. Core inflation edged up to 2.9%. Producer prices rose 6.5%, the highest in over three years. The Fed's preferred gauge, the PCE index, sits at 3.8% — nearly double the 2% target. A Reuters poll of 102 economists found that 72 now expect rates to stay unchanged for the rest of 2026, up from about half last month and a third before that. Markets are pricing in a 60% chance of a rate hike by October.

Then, over the weekend, everything shifted again. The US and Iran announced a peace deal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude dived 4.5% to $83.40 per barrel, its lowest in three months. Asian currencies and equities surged. The Indian rupee, which had been battered to near-record lows, is expected to open Monday at 94.80-94.85 per dollar, up from Friday's 95.11 close.

## What to Watch on Wednesday

**The dot plot** is the headline event. In March, the median FOMC projection showed one 25-basis-point rate cut by year-end. Nordea's Jan von Gerich expects the new dots to eliminate those projected cuts entirely, with some officials now calling for hikes. "Some calls for hikes are actually also likely to creep into the dot plot," he wrote in a note to clients.

**The statement language** will signal whether the Fed is dropping its lingering bias toward future easing. Three dissents at the April meeting already pushed for removing that language. If the June statement adopts a neutral or mildly hawkish tone, it confirms the rate-cut era is over for now.

**Warsh's press conference** is, as BMO's Michael Gregory put it, "must-see TV." Warsh has a history of pressing for rate hikes. But during his confirmation campaign, he promised rate cuts — the White House's preferred outcome. Edward Jones senior economist James McCann captured the uncertainty: "We don't really know. It could be a genuine surprise next week."

Warsh is also philosophically opposed to the Fed giving markets too much guidance. He has criticised the dot plot itself and suggested the Fed should say less, not more. If he follows through, markets will have to navigate with less forward guidance — which means more volatility in response to every economic data release.

## What This Means for NRI Money

**FCNR deposits**: Indian banks have been offering NRIs up to 7% on dollar deposits, following the RBI's measures to attract foreign inflows. If the Fed signals rates will stay elevated, those yields hold. If hike signals emerge, rates could even tick higher. Either way, the arbitrage between US and Indian rates remains attractive for NRIs with dollar income.

**Rupee trajectory**: The rupee has been under relentless pressure in 2026 — down 6% year-to-date, touching nearly 97 per dollar in May. The Iran peace deal gives it breathing room. Kotak Mahindra Bank expects the rupee to move toward 93-93.5 if oil stays near $80. But if Warsh's Fed turns hawkish and the dollar strengthens, that rally faces headwinds. The currency will whipsaw between oil relief and Fed signalling all week.

**Indian equities**: Foreign investors have been fleeing Indian stocks — nearly $18 billion in outflows in March alone. But with valuations corrected (the Nifty 50 forward PE is down to 18x from elevated levels), lower oil, and the RBI's support measures, the case for re-entry is building. A dovish-leaning Fed would accelerate foreign inflows. A hawkish pivot would delay them.

**Remittances**: Every NRI who sends money home is doing implicit currency math. At 95 rupees to the dollar, a $2,000 monthly remittance buys ₹1,90,000. At 93, it buys ₹1,86,000. That ₹4,000 difference compounds over months — and Warsh's Fed will directly influence which number families see on their transfer receipts.

## The Larger Picture

The unusual convergence of events — a new Fed chair's debut, inflation at multi-year highs, a peace deal that could reshape energy markets, and a Reserve Bank of India that has just rolled out its most aggressive inflow measures in a decade — makes this week genuinely pivotal. For the Indian diaspora, which straddles both economies, the stakes are doubled.

The FOMC decision drops Wednesday at 2 PM Eastern Time. Warsh's press conference follows at 2:30 PM. By the time markets close that afternoon, NRI investors will know whether to lean into the rupee rally, lock in dollar yields, or brace for a very different second half of 2026.
